_about: Bacterium -> bacterium metabolic relationships: who feeds whom, with what.
This is a dimension the app did not previously model at all. seed_data.json
maps condition -> taxon and symptom_data.json maps taxon -> symptom, but
nothing captured that one organism's waste product is another's substrate.
That relationship was being written as prose inside individual notes, where
it cannot be queried, drawn, or kept consistent.
Why it matters: it is the mechanism behind indirect intervention effects. A
bifidogenic prebiotic raises butyrate without feeding a single butyrate
producer directly - the effect travels along these edges. Modelling them
explicitly means the map can show second-order consequences instead of
implying an intervention touched only the taxon it was measured against.
evidence field, deliberately explicit rather than buried in prose:
in-vitro-coculture  two named organisms grown together, direct demonstration
animal              causal work in a living animal
inferred            established biochemistry, no direct study of THIS pair

edges.note: B. bifidum degrades human milk oligosaccharides and releases the constituent sugars, which F. prausnitzii uses to produce butyrate. Mechanism differs by HMO type. This is the edge behind 2'-FL raising butyrate despite F. prausnitzii not consuming 2'-FL itself.

B. infantis metabolises 2'-FL into acetate, lactate and 1,2-propanediol; E. hallii converts these to butyrate. Strain- and HMO-structure-specific - it depends which B. infantis strain and which fucosylated HMO are present. A separate report found the B. adolescentis to A. hallii butyrate link only in ADULTS, not infants.

Not a bacterium-to-bacterium edge but the same logic, and unusually well demonstrated: serum lactate crosses the epithelial barrier into the gut lumen, Veillonella converts it to propionate, and the host uses the propionate. Causal in mice - V. atypica inoculation increased exhaustive treadmill run time, and intrarectal propionate alone reproduced the gain. Exercise manufactures this genus's substrate.

Not a named-pair demonstration, but the outputs move together: in a SHIME colonic model seeded with faecal microbiota from people with severe anxiety, psilocybin raised Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while acetic, propionic and butyric acid rose 2.26-, 2.69- and 2.21-fold. Consistent with the cross-feeding edges above operating in a whole community. Caveats: alpha-diversity fell slightly and GABA DECREASED.
edges.ref: Salgaco et al. 2026, Drugs and Drug Candidates (DOI 10.3390/ddc5030046)

edges.note: B. adolescentis feeds lactate to lactate-utilising butyrate producers. The demonstration is unusually clean: E. hallii and A. caccae FAILED to grow on starch in pure culture, but in coculture with B. adolescentis butyrate was formed - so the butyrate is only possible via the cross-feed, not by the partner alone. Promotes what was previously listed as an unverified candidate.
edges.ref: Two routes of metabolic cross-feeding between Bifidobacterium adolescentis and butyrate-producing anaerobes (PMID 16672507)

edges.note: Promotes a previously unverified candidate. B. thetaiotaomicron's succinate supported P. faecium growth and propionate production, and the succinate was COMPLETELY converted to propionate - co-culture growth matched monoculture supplied with equivalent succinate. P. faecium is asaccharolytic: it barely uses carbohydrates and depends on succinate from others, so this is obligate rather than opportunistic cross-feeding. RNA-Seq showed P. faecium upregulating succinate-transport genes specifically in co-culture.
edges.ref: Ikeyama et al. 2020, MicrobiologyOpen - B. thetaiotaomicron/P. faecium co-culture + RNA-Seq (PMID 32856395)

edges.note: A second, substrate-independent route into F. prausnitzii. R. intestinalis, R. faecis and Coprococcus eutactus degrade beta-mannans (carob galactomannan, konjac glucomannan); F. prausnitzii CANNOT - it grew only on enzyme-predigested beta-mannans - but coexisted with the degraders in co-culture, with butyrate a major product. Note this makes F. prausnitzii dependent on Roseburia for this substrate class, the reverse of the direction people usually assume between two butyrate producers.
edges.ref: FEMS Microbiology Ecology 2026 - twelve-strain panel, six-strain co-cultures (PMID 42283799)

edges.note: A. muciniphila degrades host MUCUS and liberates oligosaccharides, which non-mucus-degrading butyrate producers then ferment. This is a host-derived, DIET-INDEPENDENT route to butyrate - it keeps running when dietary fibre is absent, which is why Akkermansia behaves as a keystone rather than just another SCFA producer.
edges.ref: Belzer et al. 2017, mBio - A. muciniphila co-cultured with A. caccae, E. hallii and F. prausnitzii (PMID 28928206)

edges.note: A. muciniphila degrades host MUCUS and liberates oligosaccharides, which non-mucus-degrading butyrate producers then ferment. This is a host-derived, DIET-INDEPENDENT route to butyrate - it keeps running when dietary fibre is absent, which is why Akkermansia behaves as a keystone rather than just another SCFA producer. Notably BIDIRECTIONAL with this partner: E. hallii produces pseudovitamin B12, which A. muciniphila uses to make propionate. The only reciprocal edge in this network.
edges.ref: Belzer et al. 2017, mBio - A. muciniphila co-cultured with A. caccae, E. hallii and F. prausnitzii (PMID 28928206)

edges.note: A. muciniphila degrades host MUCUS and liberates oligosaccharides, which non-mucus-degrading butyrate producers then ferment. This is a host-derived, DIET-INDEPENDENT route to butyrate - it keeps running when dietary fibre is absent, which is why Akkermansia behaves as a keystone rather than just another SCFA producer. This is a third independent route into F. prausnitzii, alongside the Bifidobacterium and Roseburia edges.
edges.ref: Belzer et al. 2017, mBio - A. muciniphila co-cultured with A. caccae, E. hallii and F. prausnitzii (PMID 28928206)

edges.note: The return leg of the Akkermansia syntrophy, and the only edge in this network pointing backwards. E. hallii supplies pseudovitamin B12 and A. muciniphila uses it to produce propionate - so the relationship is mutualistic rather than one organism simply feeding on another's waste.
edges.ref: Belzer et al. 2017, mBio - A. muciniphila co-cultured with A. caccae, E. hallii and F. prausnitzii (PMID 28928206)

edges.note: The ONLY edge where F. prausnitzii is a feeder rather than a recipient - everywhere else in this network it is fed. The pair was co-isolated and cross-feeds for growth and butyrate production. Reported mechanism is reciprocal: F. prausnitzii's lactate serves as electron donor for D. piger, and D. piger's acetate is used by F. prausnitzii for butyrate. HONEST LIMIT: the Nature abstract confirms co-isolation and cross-feeding but does not itself state the directional split or the fold-changes (butyrate ~1.5x up, lactate ~2.3x down) - those come from secondary summaries of the same work and were not confirmed against the full text.
edges.ref: Khan et al. 2023, Nature - co-isolated F. prausnitzii and D. piger, cross-feeding for growth and butyrate production (PMID 37532933)

edges.note: Return leg of the F. prausnitzii / D. piger mutualism. Uncomfortable tension worth stating: Desulfovibrio is recorded in this app as UP in Parkinson's, with hydrogen sulfide, LPS and magnetite proposed as alpha-synuclein aggregation triggers (PMID 34012926). So the same genus is a butyrate-supporting partner in vitro and a suspected neurodegeneration driver in vivo. Both can be true - species and context differ, and D. piger is not the whole genus - but it is a good reminder that a cross-feeding edge is not an endorsement.
edges.ref: Khan et al. 2023, Nature - co-isolated F. prausnitzii and D. piger, cross-feeding for growth and butyrate production (PMID 37532933)

candidates.product: methane; shifts Christensenella fermentation toward acetate
candidates.why: Interspecies H2 transfer proposed as the reason these two co-occur globally and both associate with lean BMI. Surfaced in search but NOT yet verified against the primary source.

_keystone_resource.title: Cross-feeding in the gut microbiome: Ecology and mechanisms
_keystone_resource.why: The comprehensive review to mine for the remaining network. Start here rather than running 100 ad-hoc searches.
leads_already_surfaced: Bacteroidota and Negativicutes convert succinate to propionate (supports the pending Bacteroides -> Phascolarctobacterium edge)
Anaerobutyricum hallii, Desulfovibrio piger and Coprococcus catus convert lactate to acetate/propionate/butyrate
Methanogens and acetogens remove hydrogen via methane and acetate (supports the pending Christensenella -> Methanobrevibacter edge)
